[[Open vowel|Open]] | align="center" |   | align="center" | {{IPA link|a}} {{IPA link|aː}} | align="center" |   |} Diphthongs include ''ey'' {{IPA|[ej]}}, ''ow'' {{IPA|[ow]}} and ''oow'' {{IPA|[oːw]}}. Luiseño vowels have three lengths. * [[vowel length|Short]]: The basic vowel length. In writing, this is the standard value of a given vowel, e.g. {{angbr|a}}. * [[vowel length|Long]]: The vowel is held twice as long but with no change in quality. In writing, a long vowel is often indicated by doubling it, e.g. {{angbr|aa}}. * [[vowel length|Overlong]]: The vowel is held three times as long but with no change in quality. In writing, an overlong vowel is indicated by tripling it, e.g. {{angbr|aaa}}. Overlong vowels are rare in Luiseño, typically reserved for absolutes, such as [[interjection]]s, e.g. '' '''aaa'''shisha'', roughly "haha!" (more accurately an exclamation of praise, joy or laughter). ==== Variants ==== For some native speakers recorded in ''The Sparkman Grammar of Luiseño'', the [[allophone]]s {{IPA|[ə]}} and {{IPA|[ɨ]}} are [[Free variation|free variants]] of {{IPA|[e]}} and {{IPA|[i]}} respectively. However, other speakers do not use these variants. Sparkman records fewer than 25 Luiseño words with either {{IPA|[ə]}} or {{IPA|[ɨ]}}. For one of these words (''ixíla'' "a cough") the pronunciations {{IPA|['''ə'''xɨla]}} and {{IPA|['''ɨ'''xɨla]}} are both recorded. [[Stress (linguistics)|Unstressed]] {{IPA|[u]}} freely varies with {{IPA|[o]}}. Likewise, unstressed {{IPA|[i]}} and {{IPA|[e]}} are free variants. ==== Vowel syncope ==== Vowels are often [[Syncope (phonetics)|syncopated]] when attaching certain [[affix]]es, notably the possessive prefixes ''no-'' "my", ''cham-'' "our", etc. Hence ''p'''o'''lóv'' "good", but ''o-plovi'' "your goodness"; ''kich'''u'''m'' "houses" ([[nominative case]]), but ''kichmi'' "houses" ([[accusative case]]). ==== Accent ==== A [[Stress (linguistics)|stress accent]] most commonly falls on the first [[syllable]] of a word. A single consonant between a stressed and unstressed vowel is doubled. Most are geminate, such as ''w'' {{IPA|[wː]}} and ''xw'' {{IPA|[xːʷ]}}. However, some take a glottal stop instead: ''ch'' {{IPA|[ʔt͜ʃ]}}, ''kw'' {{IPA|[ʔkʷ]}}, ''qw'' {{IPA|[ʔqʷ]}}, ''ng'' {{IPA|[ŋʔ]}}, ''th'' {{IPA|[ðʔ]}}, ''v'' {{IPA|[vʔ]}}, ''x'' {{IPA|[xʔ]}} (Elliott 1999: 14–16.) As a rule, the possessive prefixes are unstressed. The accent remains on the first syllable of the root word, e.g. {{Lang|lui|no'''kaa'''may}} "my son" and never'' *'''no'''kaamay''. One rare exception is the word ''{{Lang|lui|'''pó'''-ha}}'' "alone" (< ''po-'' "his/her/its" + ''ha'' "self"), whose invariable prefix and fixed accent suggests that it is now considered a single [[lexis (linguistics)|lexical item]] (compare ''{{Lang|lui|no'''ha'''}}'' "myself", {{Lang|lui|po'''ha'''}} "him/herself", etc.). === Consonants === Luiseño has a fairly rich [[consonant]] inventory. {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center;" |+ Luiseño consonant phonemes |- ! colspan="2" | ! However, only {{IPA|[tʃ]}} occurs intervocalically, and only {{IPA|[ʃ]}} is found preconsonantally and at word final position. Examples of these [[allophones]] in [[complementary distribution]] abound, such as ''ya{{saltillo}}ásh'' ('man {{abbr|{{sc|nom}}|nominative}}') and ''ya{{saltillo}}áchi'' ('man {{abbr|{{sc|acc}}|accusative}}'). *{{IPA|/r/}} is trilled at the beginning of a word and a tap between vowels. *The two sibilants have also been described as dental and retroflex {{IPA|[ʂ]}} (Elliott 1999: 14). == Orthography == Along with an extensive [[oral tradition]], Luiseño has a written tradition that stretches back to the [[Conquistador|Spanish settlement]] of San Diego. [[Pablo Tac]] (1822–1841), a native Luiseño speaker and Mission Indian, was the first to develop an orthography for his native language while studying in Rome to be a Catholic priest.Clifford, pp. 39-46. His orthography leaned heavily on Spanish, which he learned in his youth. Although Luiseño has no standardized spelling, a commonly accepted orthography is implemented in reservation classrooms and college campuses in San Diego where the language is taught. The alphabet taught in schools is:Raymond Basquez Sr, Neal Ibanez & Myra Masiel-Zamora (2018) ''ꞌAtáaxum Alphabet''. Great Oak Press :{{saltillo}} ꞌa ch ꞌe h ꞌi k kw l m n ng ꞌo p q qw r s ꟍ{{angbr|Ꟍ ꟍ}} were added to Unicode in 2024. Previously {{angbr|s̸}} with a combining diacritic was used. When fonts did not support that, {{angbr|ş}} was used as a substitute. sh th t ꞌu v w x xw y Current [[orthography]] marks stress with an [[acute accent]] on the stressed syllable's vowel, e.g. {{lang|lui|chil'''ú'''y}} "speak Spanish", {{lang|lui|koy'''óo'''wut}} "whale". Formerly, stress might be marked on both letters of a long vowel, e.g. {{lang|lui|koy'''óó'''wut}}, or by underlining, e.g. {{lang|lui|koyoowut}} "whale"; stress was not marked when it fell on the first syllable, e.g. {{lang|lui|h'''ii'''cha}} "what" (currently {{lang|lui|h'''íi'''cha}}). The marking of word-initial stress, like the marking of predictable glottal stop, is a response to language revitalization efforts.
